Password Protector

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A new day, a new password, a new hack. Carte Blanche spends a day with a leading software architect who will share tips on how to navigate the digital world when it comes to password safety.

Unique Selling Point:
Evan Knowles is a system architect for discovery life - although he will be speaking to us as a private expert. With artificial intelligence, computer science and an applied mathematics degrees and 15 years experience in programming, we will follow Evan for a day and learn about the world of password safety. This story will be focused on educating our audience on passwords and what is a strong password and even where the gaps are in their daily routines – like their car, open wifi, your CCTV camera and router. We will speak to Prof. Rika Butler who did a study on “The password practices applied by South African online consumers: Perception versus reality. In which she found that South Africans regard themselves as proficient in passwords, however, the reality is that they are poor at password security, password creation and with management practices with only 11% of the studies respondents able to distinguish what a strong password entails.

Summary:
Rika Butler's study: http://www.sajim.co.za/index.php/SAJIM/article/view/638
Rika has made a survey for us AND I will use this in my story. In terms of case studies I will use this test to show our own results, do some on the streets and some via survey's and also we will have a social media questionnaire before the show and give the results are the segment. Evan will be a case study as well who will take us through the various steps of password safety - please see below.

There are some international examples - like where Mark Zuckerberg was hacked, new times was hacked by China. etc.

Further information:
A DAY IN THE LIFE OF EVAN KNOWLES:
1. We wake up in the morning and open our phones - iPhone is using bio metrics (finger prints) - is this really safe? Evan says not. It's actually creating a false sense of security, because we only have 10 fingers, and the technology only reads a few main points on the thumb and that is just converted into a computer programmed language that is easy for someone to hack the string of characters and therefore is not necessarily a password safe technology (similarly with QR codes - like airplane tickets). So in South Africa the new banking system incorporating bio metrics, that the government is promoting, may not be that safe.
2. He says iPhones are safer, but Android technology is shocking when it comes to passwords, because you can download any file and install it on your phone, and because it's not through one store like Apple, this allows people to download viruses and fake apps that will send anyone your information like passwords.
3. Then there is the problem of where you keep your passwords - Evan gets to work and he has a different “no worded”, non-personal passphrase created by a password manager for every single application that needs a password. This is a randomly generated password and not a "worded pass phrase" like ILoveSnow (hackers can crack passphrases easily using dictionary attack).
4. In South Africa there have been several password breaks – like the GCIS break earlier this year - Evan can speak to this. And other examples in South Africa like the Department of Water Affairs (their passwords were so easy to crack because they were in “plain text.” Evan will give us password safety tips as consumers but also show us where the technology is going and where potential gaps may be. He says websites like computicket that send you back your password if you ask for it, run the risk of money coming out of your wallet. He says that there are different attacks: a "brute force attack”, A rainbow table attack uses computer hashes - the numerical value of an encrypted password and it runs a list of all possible password combinations with a hashing algorithm in mind. (Also social engineering and Phishing attacks).
5. Some of the gaps you may not have thought possible : Your car- Evan said new car computers that connect to your phone allow your cars system to be hacked and he suggests a strong password – please see video and article: https://www.wired.com/2015/07/hackers-remotely-kill-jeep-highway/
6. Evan also says one of the biggest threats for password hacks is when you are in a free wifi zone, because there can be a "middle man" attack meaning your phone's communication is fine, but the date has to travel through the router - and too needs a password. Evan your router without a password can be hacked. While driving to work you pass hundreds of wifi routers and should you have the same carrier he can get the username for every account and probably access your devices.
7. Did you know you need a password for your CCTV camera's in your house – Evan says there are thousands of websites dedicated to cracking people’s CCTV camera’s. Even youtube.
8. Evan doesn’t want to scare you, but he says he just wants to install a healthy sense of paranoia and for people to understand how simple it is, and help them protect themselves with strong passwords.

Press Release:


Password Protection
Do you use similar passwords for every online platform? Did you know that your home’s WiFi router (not just the signal) can be hacked? So can your CCTV cameras and many online platforms you subscribe to. That means hackers with sinister intent could be watching you or your children at any time. The average South African is largely naive to the need for secure passwords—or even what secure really means. Carte Blanche asks: Just how vulnerable are you?


Script:


The biggest landscape in South Africa is virtual: a “cyberscape” where daily life plays out digitally. When it comes to cybercrime South Africa ranks third in the world. Experts say we are easy pickings for hackers, because we aren’t password security conscious.
Evan: “You can ask yourself when you left today, I locked my door, I locked by gate, put on my alarm, what did I do for my passwords?”
Computer software developer Evan Knowles has an articifical intelligence degree and more than 15 years experience in computer programming. Surprisingly, changing your password regularly doesn’t neccessarily make you safer.
Evan: “It just makes it harder for the humans to remember, and that’s when you start seeing things like people writing their passwords down on sticky notes, so its not such a pain evey time they have to change it.”
Link: ”When we think of password security we you tend to only think of our computers, but now it includes everything around you.”
Cyber security specialist Keitumetsi Tsotetsi is well aware of the threat hackers pose when it comes to cracking your password.
K: “As technology advances, hacking advances and previously you would have had to guess, but now you have an app or a software that will sit and try to figure it out.”
Link: “With more appliances and devices having internet access, soon our entire homes will be online, your personal information is very valuable, and can be sold to the highest bidder.”
K: “Information is a big currency and if I can steal your information I can literally sell it.”
South Africans need to become more security conscious. The first step is making sure you’ve changed your default password that came with your internet router when you bought it.
Evan: “And people go, mmm that sounds pretty complicated, I’m sure it’s fine. And now we have all these routers online with a default password.”
Consumers should go so far as to question everything – even their CCTV camera security.
Evan: “You don’t think this CCTV camera comes without a password and by default to let me view this CCTV camera it puts itself on the internet. I think I’m monitoring my home, somebody else is also monitoring my home.”
Link: “In a recent study, South Africans think theyre password security conscious, but in reality, they’re not.”
Professor of Computer Science Rika Butler conducted a survey to find out whether South Africa’s consumers understood password protection.
Rika: 7.45 “About 80% of the people said that they knew exactly or had a very good idea what a strong password is… 8.00However when comparing that perception to the reality; there is a huge gap. (9.00) less than 10% of the people were actually able to rank the passwords from least to most secure. And this all points to the South African community overestimating their password knowledge.”
Rika identified several online bad habits.
Rika: “They rather choose the ease of remembering the password over the strength.
Rika: “8.50 when they create a new password or they use personal meaningful information such as maiden names, their favourite pet’s names, numbers that are familiar to them in their passwords.”
Rika: “They share passwords; they reuse the old passwords and use the same password simultaneously for more than one site.”
Rika: “20% of the people indicated that they use their internet banking password to access other computer sites as well. 11.03”
We showed these students where they were going wrong.
Miche Moonsamy: “I chose something that’s like a mix between names and numbers that were familiar to me.”
Claire: If it’s got a lot of your personal information, it’s not actually a strong password.”
Miche: “That kind of makes sense, because you always see those movies, where they like analyze a person to figure out their password.”
Cayleigh Jacobs: “I change my passwords all the time.
Claire: “That doesn’t mean that you’ve got a strong password.”
Cayleigh: “Really, okay I didn’t know that.
Claire: “Would you surpised in knowing that you’ve been creating maybe weak passwords?”
Elton Baloyi: “If somebody were to find my bank card and then they looked at me and estimated my date of birth, they could easily, you know… find something similar.
Claire: “Have you ever told anyone your one of your passwords or your pin?”
Allaster Sibanda: “Yes, unfortunately.”
Claire: “Have you ever used the same password for multiple sites?”
Allaster: “Yup, I use the same password for everything.”
This year several government websites were hacked.
Evan: “Without being logged in, from a search bar, he could add a bit of code in it, and then along with the search results would come a whole lot of user names and passwords. The passwords used there might be used somewhere else.”
Keitumetsi: “It’s so important to make sure that your password is strong, because there is also brute forcing, it’s trial and error…trying something over and over again.”
Evan: “Mark Zuckerburg, the king of social media and someone who really should know better, his account was hacked, but what made it worse is that his password was da da da da.”
Entering a second password from a text message to verify your identity is a form of two factor authentication used by banks.
Evan: “All that’s needed to steal your two factor authentication pin is from somebody to sim swap to someone else and then send the pin to them. “
Even biometric systems can provide a false sense of security.
Evan: “Although scanning a fingerprint or retina produces a very nice long password, once its converted to a digital form from your finger, it’s just another password. Except you only have 10 fingers, unless you start using your toes which is a little bit less convenient.”
Evan suggests using a password manager which generates secure keys for you.
Evan: “At least it brings the number of passwords you have to remember down to one.”
Passphrases also offer safer alternatives to passwords.
K : “a passphrase is longer, it could be a sentence, and you can use different letters as numbers.”
People should be as vigilant as they are in the real world because anyone can be a hacker’s next victim.
K: “People don’t think cyber security is a real thing until it happens to them.”
END

Some of the gaps you may not have thought possible : Your car- Evan said new car computers that connect to your phone allow your cars system to be hacked and he suggests a strong password – please see video and article: https://www.wired.com/2015/07/hackers-remotely-kill-jeep-highway/ 6. Evan also says one of the biggest threats for password hacks is when you are in a free wifi zone, because there can be a "middle man" attack meaning your phone's communication is fine, but the date has to travel through the router - and too needs a password. Evan your router without a password can be hacked. While driving to work you pass hundreds of wifi routers and should you have the same carrier he can get the username for every account and probably access your devices. 7. Did you know you need a password for your CCTV camera's in your house – Evan says there are thousands of websites dedicated to cracking people’s CCTV camera’s. Even youtube. 8. Evan doesn’t want to scare you, but he says he just wants to install a healthy sense of paranoia and for people to understand how simple it is, and help them protect themselves with strong passwords.
